title: Yara and the Missing Honey Label
markdown:
Once, in a valley where the sun painted the hills gold and the air smelled of wildflowers, lived a girl named Yara. Her aunt Mae kept a hundred busy hives, little villages of queens and workers. In the mornings the frames came in heavy, and the shed filled with a gold so slow it seemed to think. Yara loved to watch it pour into smooth glass jars. Each jar held a summer of blossoms and warm breeze. When Mae smiled, Yara’s heart felt full. The bee yard hummed like a song that never quite finished.

Every day she helped with the harvest. Jars clinked in the bottling shed. Mae would wipe a lid, hold it to the light, and nod if the seal was true. Honey made the small room smell like the coziest corner of the year. Beside the hives, tied loosely to a fence post, Dock the donkey waited. His long ears twitched while he munched clover. His eyes followed Yara with a steady affection, as predictable as the bees themselves. Sometimes she fed him a clover head from her palm and felt the warm huff of his breath, which was its own kind of answer.

Sometimes a restlessness flickered in her all the same. She would look toward the rolling hills and want an adventure a little larger than lids and labels. She never said so, not even to Dock.

Until one day a quiet fell that felt heavier than any buzzing. Mae had filled the last jar of the summer’s special honey, the one whose label promised sunshine and warm breezes, the one meant for the village harvest festival. She reached for the label. Her hand met empty air.

Mae wrung her hands. Worry gathered on her face like mist on the fields before dawn.

Yara’s eyes, usually simply curious, went focused. She knelt. Her fingers traced the dusty ground near the bottling table. “Look, Dock,” she whispered.

A faint shimmer of pollen caught the light, a tiny trail leading away from the shed. Beside it were hoofprints, not Dock’s familiar rounded ones, but smaller, daintier.

A quiet resolve settled in her, firm as an old oak’s roots. She knew those prints. She knew the deliberate path they suggested. Her gaze went past the hills to the far end of the valley, where shadows grew long.

“The oldest apple tree, Dock.”

Dock nudged her with his velvety head and made a soft rumble of understanding.

Because of that, they followed. Yara walked with care. The pollen led them past whispering reeds and over mossy stones that felt cool through her worn boots. A skylark went up and came down again, uninterested in labels. The little hoofprints were a silent guide, away from the familiar shed and into the leafy quiet of the woods. Once they stopped while Dock cropped a mouthful of clover, and Yara listened to the valley’s ordinary sounds until the trail felt like a conversation rather than a chase.

The great apple tree stood with gnarled branches and weathered bark, a witness to more seasons than anyone in the valley could count. Fallen blossom-ghosts still clung in the grass, brown now. Near its mossy roots huddled a tiny shy creature, fur the colour of dried leaves, whiskers twitching. A torn leaf house leaned in the hollow, one wall flapping. Clutched in the dormouse’s paws, gleaming in the dappled light, was the missing honey label.

The dormouse blinked dark bead eyes. Its small body trembled. Yara knelt slowly, careful not to frighten it further.

“Hello there. Are you all right?”

The dormouse held the label tighter, as if it were a shield. It was trying to patch a worn hole in a delicate leaf, using the colourful sturdy paper like a borrowed mend. It was not stealing. It was keeping the rain out. Its wide eyes told a quiet story: a home damaged by a fierce wind, and a need for something strong and bright.

Yara understood. A warmth different from the sun, sweeter than the honey, spread through her. Dock offered a rumble of empathy. From her apron she drew a smooth flat stone, worn by the stream, just the size for a patch. She held it out, hand open and steady.

The dormouse hesitated. Its nose twitched. Then it extended a paw and gave back the label.

Until finally they sat under the apple tree, Yara and Dock, in the dappled shade. The dormouse set the stone against its leaf house and pressed until the mend held. It gave a tiny squeak that sounded very like thank you, and slipped into the undergrowth.

Yara looked at the label, golden letters still bright, then thought of the jar waiting back in the shed. She did not hurry. A bee wandered past, uninterested in paper. Dock cropped a clover head. Sun moved on the moss. The leaves shifted, and that was all. She turned the label in her hands and saw, along one edge, a dormouse-sized crease, as if it had already been useful.

She smoothed the paper and, later, set it on the jar. The gold shone through, a perfect fit. The festival would have its last taste of summer.

Ever since then, Yara still loved the clink of jars and the hum of the yard, and she also watched the dusty ground for pollen trails no larger than a whisper.
